name: Acute pancreatitis

matching.reasoningTemplate: Severe epigastric pain radiating to the back with raised lipase indicates pancreatitis.

redFlags: Assess severity (organ failure) — may need ICU

clinicalPearls: Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: typical epigastric pain radiating to the back, serum lipase/amylase >=3x ULN, or characteristic findings on cross-sectional imaging (Harrison 22e p.2745).

Lipase is more pancreas-specific than amylase and is the single best enzyme to measure; it stays elevated longer (7-14 days) whereas amylase often normalises by 3-7 days (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745).
Gallstones and alcohol together account for ~80-90% of cases; gallstones are the single most common cause (30-60%), alcohol the second (15-30%) (Harrison 22e p.2744).
ALT >3x ULN strongly points to a gallstone aetiology in acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2745).

Abdominal ultrasound is the recommended initial imaging study, chiefly to assess for gallstones and bile-duct dilation; contrast CT is best deferred to ~3-5 days if the patient is not improving and is usually not needed in the first 48-72 h (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746).
Persistent organ failure (>48 h) is the most important determinant of severity; if SIRS has resolved by 24 h, organ failure or necrosis is unlikely to develop (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2748).
Hemoconcentration (hematocrit >44%) and a rising BUN are early warning signs of more severe disease and higher mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745-2748).
Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) and Grey Turner's sign (flank discoloration) are rare but signal severe necrotizing/hemorrhagic disease (Harrison 22e p.2745).
harrison.pathophysiology: Acute pancreatitis is thought to begin with autodigestion: intracellular premature activation of trypsin (via lysosomal cathepsin B colocalising with digestive zymogens) within acinar cells, which then activates other proteolytic and lipolytic enzymes (chymotrypsinogen, proelastase, phospholipase A2). A second phase recruits and sequesters leukocytes/macrophages, amplifying intrapancreatic inflammation, and a third phase results from activated enzymes and cytokines acting on distant organs, producing edema, hemorrhage, vascular damage, fat necrosis and coagulation/cellular necrosis. Release of bradykinin, vasoactive substances and histamine drives vasodilation, increased vascular permeability and edema, and can culminate in SIRS, ARDS and multiorgan failure. Pathologically the spectrum runs from interstitial (perfusion preserved, self-limited) to necrotizing pancreatitis (perfusion interrupted). Genetic susceptibility/modifier variants include PRSS1 (cationic trypsinogen), SPINK1, CFTR, CTRC, CASR and CLDN2, all converging on control of intrapancreatic trypsin activity (Harrison 22e p.2744-2745).
additionalDifferentials: Connective-tissue disorders with vasculitis (e.g., SLE, polyarteritis nodosa)
infectionMimics: Pneumonia (may present with upper abdominal pain and is in the differential of acute pancreatitis) (Harrison 22e p.2745)
nonInfectiousMimics: Diabetic ketoacidosis - abdominal pain with raised TOTAL amylase mimics pancreatitis, but lipase is often NOT elevated and pancreatic imaging is normal (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746)
Perforated peptic ulcer - can raise serum/ascitic amylase (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745)
Acute cholecystitis / biliary colic - amylase may be raised; pain is more right-sided/epigastric and ileus is usually absent (Harrison 22e p.2745)
Mesenteric ischemia/infarction - can raise ascitic-fluid amylase (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745)
Intestinal obstruction - can raise ascitic-fluid amylase; differentiated by crescendo-decrescendo pain and obstruction pattern on CT (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745)
additionalInvestigations: Serum lipase (>3x ULN) - preferred enzyme; more specific than amylase; remains elevated 7-14 days (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745)
Liver profile incl. ALT - ALT >3x ULN supports gallstone aetiology (Harrison 22e p.2745)
Serum triglycerides - to detect hypertriglyceridaemic cause (levels usually >1000 mg/dL) (Harrison 22e p.2744, p.2748)
Serum calcium - to detect hypercalcaemic cause and to monitor for hypocalcaemia (~25% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.2744-2745)
Hematocrit - hemoconcentration >44% is a severity marker (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746)
Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) at admission and 48 h - rising BUN predicts mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745, p.2748)
White cell count - leukocytosis 15,000-20,000/uL is common (Harrison 22e p.2745)
MRI/MRCP - more sensitive than CT for mild pancreatitis, necrosis, choledocholithiasis and ductal abnormalities (Harrison 22e p.2739)
EUS - useful for occult microlithiasis/biliary cause and choledocholithiasis; best performed ~4 weeks after resolution to find predisposing lesions (Harrison 22e p.2741)
Contrast-enhanced CT - to assess necrosis and local complications when not improving, ideally at 3-5 days (Harrison 22e p.2745-2746)
C-reactive protein - severity marker during hospitalization (thresholds >100 mg/L reported) (Harrison 22e p.2748)
redFlags: Persistent organ failure >48 h (respiratory, cardiovascular or renal) - hallmark of severe disease (Harrison 22e p.2746)
Modified Marshall organ-failure signs: systolic BP <90 mmHg, HR >130/min, PaO2 <60 mmHg, or creatinine >2.0 mg/dL (Harrison 22e p.2748)
BISAP score >=3 - increased in-hospital mortality (Harrison 22e p.2748)
Hemoconcentration (hematocrit >44%) and rising/admission BUN - predict severe disease and mortality (Harrison 22e p.2745-2748)
Persistent SIRS at 24 h - predisposes to organ failure and necrosis (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2748)
Pancreatic necrosis on CT - greatest mortality risk (3-10% with single-organ failure, ~50% with multiorgan failure) (Harrison 22e p.2747)
Hypoxemia (PaO2 <=60 mmHg) - may herald ARDS (Harrison 22e p.2745)
Cullen's sign / Grey Turner's sign - severe necrotizing/hemorrhagic pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2745)
Ascending cholangitis (sepsis + biliary obstruction) complicating gallstone pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2748)
harrison.prognosis: Overall mortality is low (~1%) and median hospital stay ~4 days; most cases are mild and self-limited within 3-7 days. Interstitial pancreatitis (90-95% of admissions) carries low mortality, whereas necrotizing pancreatitis (5-10%) drives most deaths. In necrotizing disease the median prevalence of organ failure exceeds 50% (slightly higher with infected vs sterile necrosis); mortality is 3-10% with single-organ failure but approaches 50% with multiorgan failure. Patients with only extrapancreatic necrosis fare better than those with pancreatic parenchymal necrosis. About 25% of patients have a recurrence, most commonly from alcohol or gallstones (Harrison 22e p.2747, p.2749).
pitfalls: Enzyme magnitude does NOT track severity - degree or serial trend of lipase/amylase does not correlate with how severe the pancreatitis is (Harrison 22e p.2745).
Serum amylase can be falsely normal or low in hypertriglyceridaemic pancreatitis, masking the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2739, p.2745).

Amylase is non-specific - raised in salivary, tubo-ovarian, pulmonary, malignant and other conditions, and spuriously high in acidemia/DKA (arterial pH <=7.32) without true pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740, p.2745).

Lipase can be mildly elevated in renal failure, and >3x ULN can occur in hepatobiliary/GI malignancy, sepsis, cirrhosis, SLE, head injury, chronic alcoholism, diabetes and post-ERCP without pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740).
Routine/early CT (within 72 h) is overused and usually unnecessary, especially in mild disease; necrosis may not be visible until several days in (Harrison 22e p.2746-2747).
Prophylactic antibiotics are NOT recommended, even in severe or necrotizing pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2746, p.2749).
Enzyme levels may be normal if blood is drawn 2-5 days after onset or if the underlying problem is chronic rather than acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2740).
harrison.severityClassification: Revised Atlanta classification (Banks et al., Gut 2013). PHASES: early (<2 weeks; severity judged clinically, not by morphology) and late (>2 weeks; imaging for local complications). SEVERITY: (1) Mild - no local complications and no organ failure (most interstitial cases; self-limited 3-7 days); (2) Moderately severe - transient organ failure (resolves <48 h) and/or local or systemic complications without persistent organ failure; (3) Severe - persistent organ failure >48 h in >=1 organ system (respiratory, cardiovascular, renal; defined by modified Marshall score >=2). MORPHOLOGY (Table 359-2): two types - interstitial (parenchymal enhancement, no necrosis) vs necrotizing (lack of parenchymal enhancement and/or peripancreatic necrosis); local collections - acute pancreatic fluid collection and pseudocyst (interstitial, pseudocyst usually >4 wk) vs acute necrotic collection (ANC) and walled-off necrosis (WON, usually >4 wk, encapsulated). SEVERITY SCORES/MARKERS (Table 359-3): BISAP >=3 (BUN >25 mg/dL, Impaired mental status/GCS<15, SIRS >=2/4, Age >60, Pleural effusion); APACHE II >=8 at 24 h; SIRS >=2 of 4 (temp <36 or >38C, HR >90, RR >20 or PCO2 <32, WCC >12,000 or <4000 or >10% bands); hematocrit >44%; admission BUN >20 mg/dL; persistent organ failure >=48 h, and pancreatic/extrapancreatic necrosis as in-hospital markers. Ranson criteria are a traditional severity index (referenced contextually).
